title: Celsus misreads Plato on the amount of evil
source_text: Ἑξῆς τούτοις τὰ διὰ πολλῶν καὶ οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτων λόγων ποικίλως ζητηθέντα περὶ φύσεως κακῶν καὶ διαφόρως ἑρμηνευθέντα δι᾿ ὀλίγων λεξειδίων οἴεται δύνασθαι ἡμᾶς μαθεῖν, φάσκων· κακὰ δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν οὔτε πρόσθεν οὔτε νῦν οὔτε αὖθις ἥττω καὶ πλείω γένοιτ᾿ ἄν· μία γὰρ ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις καὶ ἡ αὐτὴ, καὶ κακῶν γένεσις ἀεὶ ἡ αὐτή. ἔοικε δὲ καὶ ταῦτ᾿ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῷ Θεαιτήτῳ παραπεφράσθαι, ἐν οἷς ἔλεγεν ὁ παρὰ Πλάτωνι Σωκράτης· „ἀλλ᾿ οὔτε τὰ κακὰ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀπολέσθαι δυνατὸν οὔτε παρὰ θεοῖς αὐτὰ ἱδρύσθαι“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. καὶ δοκεῖ μοι μηδὲ Πλάτωνος ἀκριβῶς ἀκηκοέναι ὁ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐκπεριλαμβάνων ἐν τῷ ἑνὶ τούτῳ συγγράμματι καὶ ἐπιγράφων ἀληθῆ λόγον τὸ καθ᾿ ἡμῶν ἑαυτοῦ βιβλίον. ἡ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ λέξις φάσκουσα· „ὅταν δ᾿ οἱ θεοὶ τὴν γῆν ὕδατι καθαίρωσι“ δεδήλωκεν ὅτι καθαιρομένη ἡ γῆ τοῖς ὕδασιν ἥττονα ἔχει τὰ κακὰ παρὰ τὸν πρὸ τοῦ καθαίρεσθαι χρόνον. καὶ τοῦτό φαμεν κατὰ Πλάτωνα, τὸ ἥττονα εἶναί ποτε τὰ κακὰ, διὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ Θεαιτήτῳ λέξιν, φάσκουσαν μὴ δύνασθαι „ἀπολέσθαι ἐξ ἀνθρώπων τὰ κακά.“
pass_a_gloss: Next to these, the things inquired (ζητηθέντα) variously (ποικίλως) through many and not easily despised (εὐκαταφρονήτων) arguments (λόγων) about the nature (φύσεως) of evils (κακῶν) and interpreted (ἑρμηνευθέντα) differently, he thinks we can learn through few little phrases (λεξειδίων), saying (φάσκων): 'evils in the things that are (ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν) neither before nor now nor again (αὖθις) could become fewer (ἥττω) and more (πλείω); for one [is] the nature of the wholes (τῶν ὅλων) and the same, and the coming-to-be (γένεσις) of evils always the same'. And these seem to have been paraphrased (παραπεφράσθαι) from the things in the Theaetetus, in which Socrates in Plato said: 'but neither is it possible for evils to perish (ἀπολέσθαι) from men nor to be established (ἱδρύσθαι) among gods', and what follows. And he seems to me not even to have heard (ἀκηκοέναι) Plato accurately (ἀκριβῶς), who encompasses (ἐκπεριλαμβάνων) the truth in this one treatise (συγγράμματι) and entitles (ἐπιγράφων) his book against us True Doctrine/Word (ἀληθῆ λόγον). For the expression (λέξις) in the Timaeus saying 'when the gods cleanse (καθαίρωσι) the earth with water' has made clear that the earth cleansed by the waters has fewer evils than the time before being cleansed. And this we say according to Plato, that evils are sometimes (ποτε) fewer, because of the expression in the Theaetetus saying that 'evils' cannot 'perish from men'.
pass_b_english: After this he thinks that we can learn, from a few little phrases, what has been inquired into in many ways about the nature of evils, through many arguments not to be lightly dismissed, and has been interpreted in different ways. He says: “Evils in the things that exist could become neither fewer nor more, in the past, now, or hereafter. For the nature of the whole is one and the same, and the origin of evils is always the same.”

This too seems to have been paraphrased from what is in the Theaetetus, where Socrates in Plato says: “But it is not possible for evils to perish from among men, nor for them to be established among the gods” (Plato, Theaetetus 176a), and what follows. And it seems to me that the man who encompasses the truth in this one treatise, and gives his book against us the title True Doctrine, has not even listened to Plato carefully.

For the passage in the Timaeus that says, “When the gods cleanse the earth with water” (Plato, Timaeus 22d), has shown that the earth, when it is cleansed by the waters, has fewer evils than in the time before it was cleansed. And we say, following Plato, that evils are at times fewer, because of the passage in the Theaetetus that says that “evils” cannot “perish from among men.”

choices.choice: opening sentence reordered so 'about the nature of evils' sits with what was inquired into; οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτων -> 'not to be lightly dismissed'
Celsus's quote: removed double negative ('could not ... neither') -> 'could become neither fewer nor more, in the past, now, or hereafter'
Theaetetus 176a and Timaeus 22d checked against Plato's text

Celsus's words in the first paragraph are his own; Origen judges them a paraphrase of Plato, Theaetetus 176a (Origen's wording differs slightly from the standard text of Plato). Timaeus 22d: in Plato the gods 'cleanse the earth with waters and flood it'; Origen's quotation is shortened. Both references are certain and cited inline. 'Origin' renders γένεσις (coming-to-be), as in 4.65-66. 'Has not even listened to Plato carefully' keeps ἀκηκοέναι, which picks up Celsus's 'able to hear' at the end of 4.61. The last sentence means that Origen, on Plato's terms, speaks of evils being fewer, not of their vanishing, because the Theaetetus says they cannot perish from among men; nothing added to make this explicit. No Scripture quoted.
